option_description: Controls whether DNS zone files and configuration records have been formally labeled with a sensitivity classification (e.g., Internal Confidential, Restricted) within the organization's data governance framework. This label drives downstream handling requirements including access control, sharing restrictions, retention, and disposal.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the absence_of_sensitivity_classification_on_zone_data exposure when this attribute is false or missing. Without a classification label, zone data defaults to public or default-tier handling policies, meaning internal hostnames, service mappings, and IP-to-name bindings can be shared, retained, or exported without appropriate controls. This directly enables T1596.001 (DNS/Passive DNS) reconnaissance and T1590.002 (DNS) adversary intelligence gathering.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the organization's data classification registry or asset inventory (e.g., ServiceNow CMDB, Collibra, Microsoft Purview data catalog) and search for DNS zone files or DNS configuration records as a registered data asset. Confirm whether a sensitivity label field is populated.
how_to_obtain.navigation: ServiceNow: Navigate to Configuration > Data Classification Registry > Search 'DNS zone'. Microsoft Purview: Data Catalog > Browse Assets > Filter by 'DNS'. Collibra: Data Dictionary > Assets > Tag filter 'DNS zone'.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Asset record for DNS zone files exists with a non-empty sensitivity classification field showing a label such as 'Internal Confidential', 'Restricted', or equivalent organizational label.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether zone files or their storage directories contain classification header comments or companion metadata files (e.g., .classification or data-label.json) that record the assigned sensitivity tier, as is common in organizations using file-based classification tagging tools.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: One or more zone files contain a header comment or inline metadata referencing a classification label such as '# Classification: Internal Confidential'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the organization's DLP or data governance platform API to check whether DNS zone file assets have a classification label assigned. Example uses Microsoft Purview Information Protection REST API.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response includes a classifications array with at least one entry referencing an internal, confidential, or restricted sensitivity label.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the DNS or network infrastructure owner and the data governance team to confirm whether DNS zone data has been formally included in a data classification exercise and whether the outcome was documented in a data register or DLP policy assignment.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documented evidence (email, meeting minutes, DLP policy record) confirms DNS zone files were classified and assigned a formal sensitivity label.

typical_values: false (most common — DNS data is rarely formally classified)
true (observed in organizations with mature data governance programs or compliance mandates such as FedRAMP, ISO 27001)

option_description: Captures the data handling policy tier formally applied to DNS zone files and configuration records. The tier determines how the data is governed across its lifecycle — including who can access it, how it may be shared, how long it must be retained, and how it must be disposed of. Valid tiers range from public (least restrictive) to restricted (most restrictive).
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers absence_of_sensitivity_classification_on_zone_data when this value is 'public' or 'default', even if sensitivity_classification_assigned is true. Applying a public or default tier to DNS zone data allows it to be treated as non-sensitive operational data, enabling uncontrolled sharing with third parties, relaxed retention rules, and no formal disposal requirements — all of which expose internal topology to passive DNS reconnaissance (T1596.001) and infrastructure discovery (T1590.002).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the organization's data governance documentation, DLP policy matrix, or information classification standard to locate the policy tier mapped to DNS infrastructure data. Look for documents titled Data Classification Policy, Information Handling Standard, or equivalent.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Policy document explicitly references DNS zone files or network configuration records and assigns them to a tier such as 'internal', 'confidential', or 'restricted'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Microsoft Purview Compliance Portal, navigate to Information Protection > Sensitivity Labels and check whether a label scoped to DNS data assets exists and what protection settings are applied. In Google Workspace DLP, check Data Protection > Classification Rules for DNS-related asset rules.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Microsoft Purview: compliance.microsoft.com > Information Protection > Sensitivity Labels > Filter by 'DNS' or 'Network'. Google Workspace: admin.google.com > Security > Data Protection > Classification.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A label such as 'Confidential - Internal Network Data' or 'Restricted - Infrastructure' is listed and scoped to include DNS zone file types or storage locations.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the organization's DLP API or SIEM for data classification tag metadata associated with DNS zone file storage paths or asset identifiers.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Response lists DNS zone assets with a handling_tier value. Values of 'public' or 'default' indicate the exposure condition.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request a copy of the current DLP policy assignments from the information security or data governance team. Confirm which policy tier is active for DNS zone file storage locations or backup repositories.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Written confirmation that DNS zone data is governed under 'internal', 'confidential', or 'restricted' tier with documented handling controls.

typical_values: default (most common — inherited when no explicit classification is applied)
internal (common in organizations with basic classification programs)
confidential (observed in regulated industries or mature security programs)
public (misconfiguration — occasionally seen when DNS is treated as operational infrastructure rather than sensitive data)
restricted (rare — typically only in high-security or classified environments)

option_description: Reflects the access control posture for DNS zone transfer operations (AXFR/IXFR). Controls whether full zone data can be transferred to any requesting host, only to a defined list of authorized secondary DNS servers (enforced by IP ACLs and/or TSIG authentication), or whether zone transfers are entirely disabled. This is a critical network-level control governing bulk export of the entire DNS namespace.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers overly_broad_read_access_to_full_zone_data when this value is 'open_to_any' or 'unknown'. An unrestricted AXFR allows any internet-facing or internal host to download a complete copy of the DNS zone, exposing all internal hostnames, service names, IP mappings, and naming conventions in a single request — directly enabling T1596.001 (DNS/Passive DNS) and facilitating lateral movement planning. The absence_of_sensitivity_classification_on_zone_data rule also references this attribute as a compounding factor.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the BIND named.conf or named.conf.options file for allow-transfer directives. A value of 'any' or absence of the directive indicates open_to_any. A named ACL listing specific IPs or use of TSIG key references indicates restricted_to_named_secondaries.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: allow-transfer { <IP or key list> }; — specific IPs or TSIG keys indicate restricted_to_named_secondaries. allow-transfer { any; }; or absence of directive indicates open_to_any.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Perform a test AXFR query from an unauthorized host to confirm whether zone transfers are actually blocked at the protocol level, independent of configuration file review.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If zone transfer is restricted: 'Transfer failed' or 'REFUSED' response. If open: a full list of zone records is returned, confirming open_to_any status.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Windows DNS Server, open DNS Manager, right-click the zone, select Properties > Zone Transfers tab. For AWS Route53 private zones, check Route53 Resolver rules and VPC association settings in the AWS Console.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Windows DNS Manager: Server Manager > Tools > DNS > Expand Forward Lookup Zones > Right-click zone > Properties > Zone Transfers. AWS Console: Route53 > Hosted Zones > Select zone > View Records (AXFR is not applicable for Route53 managed zones — mark as disabled).
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Zone Transfers tab shows 'Only to the following servers' with a defined list, indicating restricted_to_named_secondaries. 'To any server' indicates open_to_any.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Windows DNS Server, use PowerShell to query zone transfer settings programmatically across all zones.
how_to_obtain.command: Get-DnsServerZone | Select-Object ZoneName, SecureSecondaries, SecondaryServers | Format-List
how_to_obtain.expected_output: SecureSecondaries value of 'TransferToSecureServers' with populated SecondaryServers list indicates restricted_to_named_secondaries. 'TransferAnyServer' indicates open_to_any.

typical_values: restricted_to_named_secondaries (target state — common in well-managed enterprise DNS)
open_to_any (common legacy finding, especially on internal BIND servers with default configs)
disabled (common for authoritative-only or stub zones with no secondaries)
unknown (common when DNS is managed by a third party or when documentation is absent)

option_description: Indicates whether a formal, written retention schedule exists specifically for DNS zone files and records. This policy must define maximum retention periods, triggers for removal when associated hosts or services are decommissioned, and documented disposal procedures for both live records and backup copies.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers indefinite_retention_of_decommissioned_dns_records when this attribute is false and stale records exist. Without a defined retention policy, DNS records accumulate indefinitely beyond the operational lifetime of their associated hosts, creating a persistent historical map of internal network topology. This enables subdomain takeover reconnaissance, passive DNS intelligence gathering (T1596.001), and IP address mapping of historical infrastructure (T1590.005). The absence_of_formal_disposal_procedure rule also relies on this attribute.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the organization's data retention schedule or records management policy from the data governance, legal, or IT GRC team. Search for DNS-specific entries or entries under 'network configuration', 'infrastructure records', or 'IT operational data'.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A retention schedule document explicitly references DNS zone files or DNS records with a defined retention period (e.g., 'DNS records retained for 90 days after host decommission') and a disposal method.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review ITSM platform (e.g., ServiceNow, Jira) decommission workflow templates for a DNS record removal step with defined timing. Confirm whether the workflow includes a step that enforces DNS record cleanup within a specified timeframe after host retirement.
how_to_obtain.navigation: ServiceNow: Workflow > Workflow Editor > Search 'decommission' or 'host retirement'. Jira: Project Settings > Workflows > Filter by 'decommission'.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Decommission workflow contains a step labeled 'Remove DNS records' or equivalent, with an assigned owner and SLA-defined completion window.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check infrastructure-as-code repositories (Terraform, Ansible, Puppet) for DNS resource definitions that include lifecycle or retention annotations, or for pipeline stages that enforce DNS record cleanup on resource destruction.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: IaC code contains lifecycle blocks or pipeline stages that explicitly destroy DNS records when associated infrastructure is deprovisioned.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the organization's document management system (SharePoint, Confluence) for a DNS or network data retention policy document. Search for 'DNS retention', 'zone file lifecycle', or 'network record disposal'.
how_to_obtain.navigation: SharePoint: Search bar > 'DNS retention policy'. Confluence: Space Search > 'DNS lifecycle' or 'zone file retention'.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A policy document dated within the last 2 years explicitly covers DNS record retention with defined periods and disposal procedures.

typical_values: false (most common — DNS-specific retention policies are rarely documented separately from general IT records policies)
true (observed in organizations subject to FedRAMP, PCI-DSS, or with mature ITSM-driven lifecycle management)

option_description: Quantifies the number of DNS records in the zone that reference hosts, services, or IP ranges that have been confirmed as decommissioned or no longer operational. This count is derived by cross-referencing zone contents against the authoritative asset inventory or CMDB decommission records.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers indefinite_retention_of_decommissioned_dns_records when this value is greater than 0 and either the retention policy is absent or automated cleanup is disabled. Stale records create a persistent historical topology map that adversaries can exploit for subdomain takeover (dangling DNS), passive DNS reconnaissance (T1596.001), and historical IP address mapping (T1590.005). A high count amplifies the reconnaissance value of zone data even after infrastructure changes.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Export the current DNS zone and cross-reference hostnames against the CMDB or asset inventory using a scripted comparison. This example uses dig for zone export and a Python script to match against a decommissioned hosts list.
how_to_obtain.command: dig @<dns-server> <zone> AXFR | grep -E '^[a-zA-Z0-9]' | awk '{print $1}' > /tmp/dns_records.txt && comm -12 <(sort /tmp/dns_records.txt) <(sort /tmp/decommissioned_hosts.txt) | wc -l
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An integer representing the number of DNS hostnames that appear in both the current zone and the decommissioned hosts list. Zero indicates no stale records.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Windows DNS environments, use PowerShell to export all DNS records and check for entries pointing to IP addresses not present in the active DHCP scope or IPAM system.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: CSV output of all A records. Cross-reference against CMDB or IPAM to identify IPs assigned to decommissioned assets.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the cloud DNS provider API to list all records and cross-reference against a decommission tracker or CMDB API. Example uses AWS Route53.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON list of A records. Compare IPs against AWS EC2 active instance inventory: aws ec2 describe-instances --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].PrivateIpAddress' to identify orphaned entries.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In InfoBlox or BlueCat IPAM/DDI platforms, use the built-in Stale Record or Orphaned DNS Record report to retrieve a count of DNS records with no associated active IP lease or CMDB match.
how_to_obtain.navigation: InfoBlox: Grid > DNS > Reports > Stale Resource Records. BlueCat: Administration > Reports > DNS Health > Orphaned Records.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A numeric report output listing DNS records with no corresponding active IP assignment or CMDB entry, providing the stale record count directly.

typical_values: 0 (ideal state — achieved only with automated cleanup or recent audit)
1–20 (common in small environments with periodic manual review)
20–200 (typical in medium enterprises without automated cleanup)
200+ (common in large, long-running environments without lifecycle management — high-risk finding)

option_description: Indicates whether an automated mechanism actively removes or flags DNS records when the associated host or service is decommissioned. This includes ITSM workflow automation, CI/CD pipeline destroy stages, infrastructure-as-code lifecycle hooks, or API-driven integrations that trigger DNS record deletion upon host retirement.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers indefinite_retention_of_decommissioned_dns_records when this attribute is false and stale records exist. Without automation, DNS cleanup depends entirely on manual processes that are frequently skipped, delayed, or forgotten during decommission workflows. This allows stale records to accumulate, enabling subdomain takeover reconnaissance and persistent network topology exposure via T1596.001 passive DNS and T1590.005 IP address mapping.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review decommission runbooks and ITSM workflow templates in ServiceNow, Jira Service Management, or BMC Remedy. Confirm whether a DNS record removal task is present as a mandatory, automated step (not just a checklist item requiring human action).
how_to_obtain.navigation: ServiceNow: Workflow Editor > Search 'decommission' > Inspect activities for automated DNS API call steps. Jira: Project > Workflows > Transitions > Check for automated post-functions targeting DNS systems.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Workflow contains an automated activity (not a manual approval step) that calls a DNS API or runs a script to delete records upon host retirement, with documented execution logs.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect Terraform, Ansible, or Pulumi infrastructure-as-code repositories for DNS resource definitions that use lifecycle blocks or are paired with destroy provisioners that remove DNS records when the parent resource is destroyed.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: IaC resource definition for DNS records includes lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true } or a destroy-time provisioner that removes the DNS entry when the associated compute resource is deprovisioned.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check CI/CD pipeline definitions (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins) for pipeline stages that execute DNS record deletion as part of infrastructure teardown workflows.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Pipeline file contains a stage referencing DNS management tool (e.g., aws route53 change-resource-record-sets with DELETE action) triggered on infrastructure teardown.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review DNS change audit logs or ITSM closure records for decommission tickets completed in the last 90 days. Verify that DNS record deletion events correlate with host decommission events within an acceptable SLA window, indicating automation is functioning.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: DNS audit log shows DELETE operations timestamped within hours of corresponding ITSM decommission ticket closures, confirming automated cleanup is functioning.

typical_values: false (most common — DNS cleanup is typically a manual checklist item in decommission runbooks)
true (observed in organizations using Infrastructure-as-Code with Terraform destroy lifecycles or mature ITSM integrations with DNS API automation)

option_description: Controls whether backup copies, exported zone file snapshots, and zone files stored on disk are encrypted on the underlying storage medium. This includes filesystem-level encryption (LUKS, BitLocker), backup tool encryption (Veeam, Bacula), object storage encryption (S3 SSE, Azure Blob encryption), or NAS/SAN volume encryption for any storage location holding DNS zone data.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers zone_file_snapshots_stored_without_encryption_at_rest when this attribute is false. Unencrypted zone file backups expose the complete DNS namespace to any party with physical or logical access to the storage medium — including storage administrators, backup operators, cloud storage bucket viewers, or attackers who compromise backup infrastructure. This is analogous to a credential store dump (T1003.003) for network topology data and directly enables full passive DNS intelligence gathering (T1596.001) without querying the live DNS service.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether the filesystem or block device hosting zone file backups uses LUKS encryption on Linux. Identify the mount point for zone backups and verify encryption status.
how_to_obtain.command: lsblk -o NAME,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINT,SIZE | grep -E 'crypto_LUKS|crypt' && cryptsetup status $(lsblk -o NAME,MOUNTPOINT | grep '/var/backup/dns\|/backup/named' | awk '{print $1}')
how_to_obtain.expected_output: lsblk output shows FSTYPE of 'crypto_LUKS' for the partition hosting DNS backups. cryptsetup status returns 'is active' for the mapped device.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For AWS S3-hosted zone file backups, verify server-side encryption is enabled on the target bucket and that the bucket policy denies unencrypted uploads.
how_to_obtain.command: aws s3api get-bucket-encryption --bucket <dns-backup-bucket-name> && aws s3api get-bucket-policy --bucket <dns-backup-bucket-name> | python3 -m json.tool | grep -A5 'Deny'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: get-bucket-encryption returns ServerSideEncryptionConfiguration with AES256 or aws:kms rule. Bucket policy includes a Deny statement for s3:PutObject without encryption headers.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Windows-based DNS backup storage, check BitLocker status on the backup drive via the Control Panel or PowerShell. For Azure Blob storage, verify encryption settings in the Azure Portal.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Azure Portal: Storage Accounts > Select backup account > Security + Networking > Encryption. Verify 'Encryption type' shows Microsoft-managed keys or Customer-managed keys.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: BitLocker reports 'Protection Status: Protection On' for the backup volume. Azure Portal shows encryption enabled with a key source configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect backup tool configuration files (e.g., Bacula bacula-dir.conf, Amanda amanda.conf, restic repository config) for encryption settings applied to DNS backup jobs.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Backup configuration contains encryption directives such as 'Encryption = yes', 'cipher = AES-256', or a non-empty passphrase/key reference for the job covering DNS backup paths.

typical_values: false (common — DNS backup encryption is frequently overlooked even when general backup encryption policies exist)
true (observed in cloud-native environments using S3 SSE by default, or in organizations with full-disk encryption on backup servers)

option_description: Controls whether access to the storage locations containing DNS zone file snapshots and backups is limited to explicitly named, authorized roles or accounts via enforced access controls. This includes POSIX filesystem permissions, NAS ACLs, S3 bucket policies, IAM roles, or equivalent mechanisms that prevent unauthorized users from reading zone file backup content.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers zone_file_snapshots_stored_without_encryption_at_rest when zone_file_encryption_at_rest_enabled is true but this attribute is false — because encryption alone is insufficient if overly broad access controls allow unauthorized users to mount or access the decrypted files. Unrestricted access to zone snapshots allows any compromised account in a broad permission group to retrieve a complete DNS namespace inventory without triggering live DNS query logs, enabling full T1596.001 passive DNS intelligence gathering and infrastructure mapping (T1590.002).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect POSIX filesystem permissions on the DNS zone backup directory to verify that read access is limited to the DNS administrator account or backup service account, and not granted to world-readable or broad group-readable permissions.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Files show permissions of 640 or 600 with owner set to named, bind, or dns-admin. Group ownership limited to a DNS admin group. No world-readable (o+r) permissions present.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For AWS S3 storage, retrieve the bucket ACL and bucket policy to confirm that public access is blocked and that only specific IAM roles or accounts are granted GetObject permissions on the DNS backup bucket.
how_to_obtain.command: aws s3api get-bucket-acl --bucket <dns-backup-bucket> && aws s3api get-bucket-policy --bucket <dns-backup-bucket> | python3 -m json.tool && aws s3api get-public-access-block --bucket <dns-backup-bucket>
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ACL shows no public grants. Bucket policy lists only specific IAM role ARNs with s3:GetObject permission. PublicAccessBlock shows all four block settings as true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For NAS/SAN storage, review share permissions in the NAS management console (e.g., NetApp ONTAP System Manager, Synology DSM, TrueNAS) for the share hosting DNS zone backups.
how_to_obtain.navigation: NetApp ONTAP: Storage > Volumes > Select DNS backup volume > Access > NFS/SMB Exports > Permissions. Synology DSM: Control Panel > Shared Folder > Select DNS backup > Permissions tab. TrueNAS: Storage > Pools > DNS backup dataset > Edit Permissions.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Share permissions list only specific DNS admin or backup service accounts with read access. No 'Everyone', 'Authenticated Users', or 'Domain Users' entries with read permission.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, use icacls to inspect ACLs on the DNS backup directory and confirm access is limited to DNS administrators and backup service accounts.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output lists only explicit entries for DNS-Admins group, backup service account (e.g., SVC_BACKUP), and SYSTEM. No entries for 'Everyone', 'Authenticated Users', 'Domain Users', or 'BUILTIN\Users'.

typical_values: false (common — DNS backup directories often inherit broad filesystem permissions from parent directories or default backup software configurations)

true (observed in environments with enforced least-privilege file system policies, cloud environments using IAM-controlled S3 buckets, or organizations that have conducted explicit backup access reviews)

option_description: Indicates whether principals granted access to DNS zone data receive read access to entire zone files or only to scoped subsets of records. This attribute directly measures whether need-to-know is enforced on zone data access controls.
security_impact: The Rego policy flags overly_broad_read_access_to_full_zone_data when zone_access_scope is full_zone or unknown. Full zone access means any compromised account in the permission group gains a complete internal network map without needing to query the live DNS service incrementally. The unknown default value means unreviewed systems automatically trigger the exposure, reflecting the principle that unverified access scope is treated as a risk.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On BIND DNS servers, review the allow-transfer and allow-query ACL directives in named.conf to determine whether zone access is granted to any/all or restricted to specific IP ranges and key-based principals.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'allow-transfer { none; }' or named ACLs with specific IPs indicates scoped_subset; 'allow-transfer { any; }' or absence of restrictions indicates full_zone.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Windows Server DNS Manager, right-click a zone, select Properties, then the Zone Transfers tab. Review whether zone transfers are disabled, restricted to specific servers, or open. Also check Active Directory DNS integrated zones for ACL inheritance in Active Directory Users and Computers.
how_to_obtain.navigation: DNS Manager > Forward Lookup Zones > [Zone Name] > Properties > Zone Transfers tab; also check Security tab for object-level ACLs
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Only specific servers listed under 'Only to the following servers' indicates scoped_subset; 'To any server' indicates full_zone.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For AWS Route 53, review IAM policies and resource-based policies to determine whether principals are granted route53:ListResourceRecordSets on specific hosted zone ARNs or on wildcard resources. Check for policies granting arn:aws:route53:::hostedzone/* scope.
how_to_obtain.command: aws iam list-policies --scope Local --query 'Policies[*].Arn' --output text | xargs -I{} aws iam get-policy-version --policy-arn {} --version-id $(aws iam get-policy --policy-arn {} --query 'Policy.DefaultVersionId' --output text) --query 'PolicyVersion.Document'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Policies referencing specific hosted zone ARNs indicate scoped_subset; wildcard resource permissions indicate full_zone.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For PowerDNS deployments, inspect the pdns.conf and any pipe or gmysql backend configurations for default-api-rectify and API key scope settings. Check whether API access grants full zone enumeration.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: API enabled with unrestricted zone listing confirms full_zone; backend-level row filtering or API key scope restrictions indicate scoped_subset.

typical_values: full_zone
unknown
scoped_subset

option_description: Determines whether non-human identities such as service accounts, CI/CD pipeline accounts, or automation scripts are members of the permission group that holds broad read access to zone data. Service accounts amplify blast radius because they are often less protected and their compromise is harder to detect.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers overly_broad_read_access_to_full_zone_data when zone_access_scope is full_zone AND this attribute is true, representing a compounded risk. A compromised service account in the broad zone read group gives an attacker automated, persistent access to the full DNS namespace. Service accounts often lack MFA, rotate credentials infrequently, and are targeted specifically because they have broad, predictable permissions.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows environments using Active Directory, enumerate members of the DNS zone read group and filter for service account naming conventions or accounts with non-expiring passwords, which are indicators of service accounts.
how_to_obtain.command: Get-ADGroupMember -Identity 'DNS Zone Readers' -Recursive | ForEach-Object { Get-ADObject -Identity $_.DistinguishedName -Properties PasswordNeverExpires,ServicePrincipalNames | Select-Object Name,ObjectClass,PasswordNeverExpires,ServicePrincipalNames }
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Accounts with PasswordNeverExpires=True or non-empty ServicePrincipalNames within the group confirm the attribute is true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For BIND ACL-based access, identify the IP addresses and TSIG keys authorized in allow-transfer and allow-query directives, then cross-reference with CMDB or infrastructure records to identify automated systems.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: TSIG key names matching CI/CD or automation naming patterns (e.g., 'jenkins-key', 'ansible-transfer') confirm service account presence.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For AWS Route 53 or GCP Cloud DNS, list IAM service accounts and roles that have zone read permissions. Check for service account emails (ending in .iam.gserviceaccount.com or with AWS role patterns) in the policy bindings.
how_to_obtain.command: aws iam get-account-authorization-details --filter LocalManagedPolicy --query 'Policies[*]' | python3 -c "import sys,json; data=json.load(sys.stdin); [print(p) for p in data if 'route53' in str(p).lower()]"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Role ARNs containing 'service-role', 'automation', or 'pipeline' patterns assigned zone read permissions confirm the attribute is true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the access review documentation for DNS zone read permissions from the identity team. Ask specifically whether the last access certification identified and removed service accounts, and whether CI/CD pipelines require DNS zone read access as part of their documented function.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Absence of recent access certification or confirmation that deployment pipelines hold zone read access confirms the attribute is true.

typical_values: true
false

option_description: Controls whether DNS query logs and diagnostic exports have hostname and internal IP address fields anonymized, pseudonymized, or masked before transmission to third-party platforms or log aggregation systems. When enabled, sensitive internal naming conventions are obscured prior to leaving the classification boundary.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires no_masking_of_internal_host_metadata_in_logs_and_exports when dns_logs_shared_with_third_party is true AND dns_log_anonymization_enabled is false. Without anonymization, DNS query logs exported to external SIEMs or monitoring vendors contain resolved hostnames and internal IPs that directly expose network topology. The default value is false, meaning systems that have never been explicitly configured for anonymization automatically represent this exposure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the syslog forwarder, Fluentd, Logstash, or Vector pipeline configuration for DNS log sources to identify whether a field transformation, masking filter, or anonymization plugin is applied to hostname and IP fields before the output stage.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Filter blocks containing mutate, anonymize, or gsub operations on hostname/IP fields confirm anonymization is enabled; absence of any transform on these fields confirms it is disabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review Fluentd or td-agent configuration files for DNS log pipelines and check for record_transformer or anonymize directives applied to host-related fields before the match output block.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Matching lines referencing DNS-related pipeline stages confirm anonymization is applied; no results confirms the attribute is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Sample recent DNS query log exports destined for third-party systems and inspect whether hostname fields contain actual internal FQDN values or tokenized/hashed representations. Check the last 100 lines of the export file or stream.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Internal FQDNs visible in plaintext (e.g., host1.corp.internal) confirm anonymization is disabled; hashed tokens or absence of recognizable hostnames suggest anonymization may be applied.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the log pipeline owner or SIEM integration team. Ask whether the DNS log export schema has been reviewed for sensitive field content and whether any data minimization or masking requirement was applied during third-party integration setup.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Confirmation that no masking transform was implemented, or that the integration was set up without a data classification review, confirms the attribute is false.

typical_values: false
true

option_description: Identifies whether DNS query logs or diagnostic exports containing resolved hostnames and internal IP addresses are transmitted to external parties, including third-party monitoring vendors, managed SOC providers, or external log aggregation platforms such as Splunk Cloud, Datadog, or Elastic Cloud.
security_impact: This attribute is the prerequisite condition in the Rego policy for no_masking_of_internal_host_metadata_in_logs_and_exports. When true, it gates both the anonymization check and the data sharing control check. Sharing DNS logs externally without controls transfers internal network topology intelligence outside the organization's classification boundary, creating a secondary attack surface at the third-party and violating the principle of data minimization.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect DNS server export configurations and log pipeline output destinations. Review syslog forwarding rules, Fluentd output plugins, and Logstash output blocks for external endpoint addresses (non-RFC1918 IPs, external domain names, or cloud service endpoints).
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output directives pointing to external IPs or cloud service endpoints (e.g., inputs.logdna.com, http-inputs.splunk.com) confirm dns_logs_shared_with_third_party is true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check active network connections from DNS servers to identify ongoing log streams to external destinations. Look for persistent TCP connections from the DNS host to external monitoring platform ports.
how_to_obtain.command: ss -tnp | grep -E '(named|syslog|fluentd|logstash|vector|filebeat)'; netstat -tnp 2>/dev/null | grep -E '443|9997|10514|5044' | grep ESTABLISHED
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Established connections to non-RFC1918 addresses on log shipping ports (5044, 9997, 10514, 443) from log forwarder processes confirm log sharing with external parties.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For cloud DNS providers, check whether diagnostic logging is enabled and where logs are routed. For AWS Route 53, verify whether query logging is enabled and whether the associated CloudWatch Log Group has a subscription filter sending to an external destination.
how_to_obtain.command: aws route53 list-query-logging-configs --query 'QueryLoggingConfigs[*].{Zone:HostedZoneId,LogGroup:CloudWatchLogsLogGroupArn}'; aws logs describe-subscription-filters --log-group-name /aws/route53/query --query 'subscriptionFilters[*].destinationArn'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Subscription filter destination ARNs pointing to Kinesis Firehose with external delivery stream targets or Lambda functions that forward externally confirm the attribute is true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review vendor contracts and the organization's SIEM or monitoring platform inventory. Ask the security operations team whether DNS query logs are included in the data sources forwarded to any managed service provider or cloud-hosted log platform.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Confirmation that DNS query logs are listed as a data source in a third-party monitoring contract or SIEM integration document confirms the attribute is true.

typical_values: true
false

option_description: Indicates whether a formal control such as a Data Processing Agreement, data classification policy addendum, or technical access restriction governs the transmission of DNS log data to external parties. This covers contractual obligations, technical enforcement mechanisms, and documented data handling requirements imposed on recipients.
security_impact: The Rego policy for no_masking_of_internal_host_metadata_in_logs_and_exports triggers independently when dns_logs_shared_with_third_party is true AND third_party_data_sharing_control_exists is false. Even if anonymization is applied, the absence of a formal governing control means there is no enforceable obligation on the third party regarding handling, retention, or onward sharing of DNS topology data. The default value of false means organizations that have never formally reviewed third-party DNS data sharing are exposed.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request copies of all Data Processing Agreements and vendor contracts for third-party monitoring platforms that receive DNS log data. Verify whether these agreements explicitly reference DNS query logs or internal network topology data as a covered data category with handling restrictions.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A DPA or contract amendment explicitly listing DNS query log data with handling, retention, and sub-processing restrictions confirms the control exists.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the organization's data classification policy and any data flow documentation for the DNS log export pipeline. Check whether the pipeline design document references a specific data sharing authorization or classification review approval.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A signed data flow authorization document or DPA reference number in the pipeline design confirms the control exists; absence of any such reference confirms it is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the third-party monitoring platform's administrative portal, check whether data residency, data retention, and access restriction settings have been configured per a contractual obligation. For Datadog, review Organization Settings > Data Governance; for Splunk Cloud, check the Cloud Services Agreement addendum.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Datadog: Organization Settings > Security > Data Governance; Splunk Cloud: Admin > Licensing and Usage > Data Governance settings
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configured data retention limits and access restriction acknowledgments in the vendor portal corroborate the existence of a governing control.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Consult the legal or privacy team to determine whether DNS log data flows to third parties were included in the organization's Record of Processing Activities or similar data inventory. Ask whether a Transfer Impact Assessment was conducted for cross-border DNS log transfers.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Inclusion of DNS log transfers in the ROPA with a DPA reference and completed TIA confirms the control exists.

typical_values: false
true

option_description: Indicates whether an approved, documented procedure exists for purging decommissioned DNS records and all associated zone data from every storage location, including the live DNS service, backup snapshots, audit logs, and exported copies. A complete procedure includes a scheduled purge cadence for zone file backups, not just removal from the active zone.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires absence_of_formal_disposal_procedure_for_dns_record_data when formal_dns_disposal_procedure_documented is false. Records removed from live DNS but retained in backups and audit logs provide adversaries with historical network topology through passive DNS reconnaissance. The default value of false means organizations that have never formally created this procedure are flagged, reflecting that undocumented disposal is equivalent to no disposal from a governance perspective.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the organization's data management policy, DNS operational runbook, and any decommissioning checklist from the DNS operations team. Verify whether any of these documents contain an explicit section covering DNS record disposal that references backup snapshot purging and audit log retention limits.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A policy document section titled 'DNS Record Disposal' or 'Zone Data Purge Procedure' with defined steps and a named backup purge schedule confirms the procedure is documented.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check backup retention configuration files for DNS-specific retention schedules. Review backup agent policies (e.g., Veeam, NetBackup, Bacula) for zone file backup jobs to determine whether a defined expiry or purge window is configured.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A backup job for zone files with an explicit Volume Retention or purge policy setting confirms that at least the backup purge schedule component exists; absence confirms the gap.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search organizational documentation repositories, wikis, or SharePoint for DNS disposal procedure documents. Also check whether any scheduled jobs exist that automate zone file backup expiry.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Matching cron entries or script files with DNS disposal logic confirm partial procedural automation; absence of both scripts and documentation confirms the attribute is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the DNS operations lead and backup administrator jointly. Ask specifically whether a decommissioned host's DNS records are tracked through a formal ticket or change management process that includes a disposal checklist covering backups and log exports, and whether this process has been tested or audited.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Reference to a specific IT Service Management ticket template or change record type with DNS disposal steps confirms the procedure is documented; inability to produce such a template confirms it is false.

typical_values: false
true
